title: A Slave Welcomed as Brother
summary: Paul asks Philemon to welcome his returning slave Onesimus, now converted, as a beloved brother, and offers to bear Onesimus’s debt himself.
historicalContext: Paul writes as a prisoner, most probably during his first Roman custody about A.D. 60–62, to Philemon, a believer of some means at Colossae whose home hosted a congregation. Onesimus, a slave of that household, had left his master, apparently without leave and possibly with property that was not his, and had come into contact with Paul, through whom he believed. Roman law treated slaves as property; a master could punish a fugitive severely, and slaves made up a large share of the empire’s population, serving as laborers, stewards, tutors, and household staff. The letter traveled with Tychicus and Onesimus alongside the letter to the Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9), and the same companions send greetings in both. Into a world where a returning runaway expected the lash, Paul sends Onesimus home carrying a letter that calls him brother.
literaryContext: Philemon is Paul’s shortest letter and follows the ordinary shape of ancient correspondence: greeting (1:1-3), thanksgiving (1:4-7), the body of the appeal (1:8-20), and closing remarks and greetings (1:21-25). Though written to one man, it is addressed also to a household church, so the request is heard by the congregation. The appeal is carefully built. Words planted in the thanksgiving—love, fellowship, refresh, heart, brother—return in the body to carry the request. Paul declines to command, holds back Onesimus’s name until the end of a sentence, plays on its meaning “useful,” and borrows the language of the ledger when he offers to pay. The letter belongs beside Colossians, whose household instructions (Colossians 3:22-4:1) and declaration that in Christ there is “neither bond nor free” (Colossians 3:11) form its immediate background.
themes: Gospel kinship that crosses social rank
Love that appeals rather than commands
Substitution and the bearing of another’s debt
The gospel undermining slavery from within

outline.title: Greeting to a Household Church
outline.summary: Paul, a prisoner, greets Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the congregation in Philemon’s home with grace and peace.

outline.title: Thanksgiving for Refreshing Love
outline.summary: Paul thanks God for Philemon’s faith and love toward all saints and prays that their shared faith will become active.

outline.title: An Appeal for Paul’s Child
outline.summary: Declining to command, Paul appeals in love for Onesimus, his convert, whom he sends back though he wished to keep him.

outline.title: Receive Him as Myself
outline.summary: Paul reads the separation as possibly providential, asks that Onesimus be welcomed as a brother, and takes his debt on himself.

outline.title: Confidence, Hope, and Greetings
outline.summary: Paul expresses confidence that Philemon will do more than asked, requests lodging, sends greetings, and closes with grace.

verses.bibleText: Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul opens without his usual apostolic title. In letters where his authority was questioned he leads with “apostle,” but here, writing to a friend and planning to ask rather than order, he calls himself “a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” The chain was real; he was under guard, most likely in Rome awaiting his hearing before Caesar (Acts 28:16, 30). Yet the phrase explains whose prisoner he is. Rome held the keys, but Christ’s cause had placed him there, and Christ’s purpose governed even his confinement. There is also fitting pathos in the title: a man whose own movements are controlled by another is about to plead for a slave whose life was legally owned by his master.

Timothy is joined to the greeting as “our brother.” Philemon probably knew him from the long ministry in Ephesus, only a few days’ journey from Colossae (Acts 19:10, 22). Timothy is not presented as a coauthor so much as a companion who shares the concern and adds his presence to the request. His title also introduces the family vocabulary that runs through the whole letter. “Brother” will be applied to Philemon (Philemon 1:7, 20) and then, decisively, to Onesimus (Philemon 1:16). Paul establishes a household word before he asks Philemon to extend it to someone new.

Philemon is “our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer.” The first term speaks of affection, the second of shared service. Philemon had likely come to faith through Paul (Philemon 1:19), and he had since put his home and resources to work for the gospel in his city. Paul is not flattering him. He names what is true and what the coming appeal will rest upon. Before Philemon hears what is asked of him, he is reminded that he stands inside a circle of love and labor whose center is Christ, and that every request made within that circle comes from those who belong to the same Lord.

wordNotes.term: δέσμιος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ (desmios Christou Iēsou) — a prisoner of Jesus Christ
wordNotes.explanation: Desmios is a person in bonds, a literal prisoner. The genitive identifies the one to whom Paul belongs in his imprisonment: he is held for Christ’s sake and under Christ’s ownership, so that his chains become part of his service rather than a defeat of it.

wordNotes.term: συνεργῷ (synergō) — fellowlabourer
wordNotes.explanation: A coworker, one who works alongside another in a common task. Paul uses it for those who shared actively in gospel work, whether traveling with him or building up local churches, and it places Philemon on the same level as Paul’s trusted associates.

verses.bibleText: And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The address widens to include “our beloved Apphia.” The best manuscripts read “our sister,” the family word Christians used for one another. Apphia was most likely Philemon’s wife. In a Greco-Roman household the mistress commonly oversaw the domestic slaves, so the return of Onesimus touched her directly. Paul names her with dignity, as a full member of the family of faith whose judgment mattered, at a time when wider society often treated women as an extension of their husbands.

Archippus is called “our fellowsoldier.” He may have been the son of the household, though his title points chiefly to his role in ministry. Paul uses the same military image for Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:25), picturing those who share hardship and conflict for the gospel. Colossians 4:17 adds a charge that Archippus fulfill the ministry he had received in the Lord, which suggests he carried real responsibility in the Colossian church, perhaps while Epaphras was away with Paul.

Finally Paul greets “the church in thy house.” The pronoun is singular and refers to Philemon, whose home was large enough to host the believers for worship, Scripture reading, prayer, and the shared meal (compare Romans 16:5; Colossians 4:15). The inclusion is deliberate. This is a personal letter, but it is not a private one. Philemon will decide about Onesimus in the presence of the congregation, and the congregation will have to receive Onesimus as well. In the body of Christ a believer’s treatment of another believer is never only a household affair; it concerns the whole family of God, which both supports and holds accountable those who belong to it.

wordNotes.term: τῇ κατ’ οἶκόν σου ἐκκλησίᾳ (tē kat’ oikon sou ekklēsia) — the church in thy house
wordNotes.explanation: Ekklēsia here is the local assembly of believers, and kat’ oikon locates it in a private home. Early Christians had no dedicated buildings, so households with room became gathering places. The church was a family meeting under one roof, where masters and slaves sat together before the same Lord.

wordNotes.term: συστρατιώτῃ (systratiōtē) — fellowsoldier
wordNotes.explanation: A comrade in arms, one who serves in the same campaign. Paul applies the image to coworkers who endure hardship for the gospel, stressing shared loyalty to one commander and shared exposure to opposition.

verses.bibleText: Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s customary greeting carries special weight in this letter. “Grace” is God’s free, undeserved favor shown in the gift of his Son; “peace” is the reconciled relationship and settled wholeness that grace creates. Both come “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,” the Son named beside the Father as the one source of these blessings. The plural “you” embraces Philemon, his household, and the whole church that will hear the letter.

Everything Paul goes on to ask is grace and peace put into practice. Philemon has received favor he never earned; he will be asked to show favor to a slave who has not earned it either. He has been brought into peace with God; he will be asked to make peace with the man who wronged him. The gospel that reconciles Jew and Gentile into one body (Ephesians 2:14-16) is about to reconcile master and slave in one house church. The greeting is no formality—it sets out the ground on which the whole appeal stands.

wordNotes.term: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη (charis hymin kai eirēnē) — grace to you, and peace
wordNotes.explanation: Paul adapts the ordinary Greek greeting into a gospel blessing and joins it with the Hebrew hope of shalom. Grace names God’s giving in Christ; peace names its fruit in restored relationship with God and with one another.

verses.bibleText: I thank my God, making mention of thee always in my prayers,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
From the whole church the address narrows to Philemon alone; the pronouns are singular from here almost to the end. Paul says, “I thank my God,” with a personal possessive that reflects his own walk with God. “Always” belongs with the thanksgiving: whenever Paul prays for Philemon, gratitude marks the prayer. Even in chains Paul kept a regular habit of intercession that included individual believers by name.

The thanks go to God, not to Philemon. The good Paul has heard about in Philemon’s life is the fruit of God’s working, so God receives the gratitude. This thanksgiving does prepare the way for the request, but it is not a device. Paul could not ask Philemon to receive Onesimus without first standing with Philemon before God. Prayer by name binds people together, and a relationship nourished by intercession is able to bear a difficult request. Those who would correct or counsel others do well to pray for them first and to thank God for what he has already done in them.

wordNotes.term: μνείαν σου ποιούμενος (mneian sou poioumenos) — making mention of thee
wordNotes.explanation: To make mention is to remember someone by name in prayer. The phrase recurs in Paul’s thanksgivings and shows that his prayers were specific, bringing particular people and their needs before God.

verses.bibleText: Hearing of thy love and faith, which thou hast toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all saints;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s thanksgiving rests on what he has heard. The report most likely came through Epaphras, the founder of the Colossian church who was now with Paul (Colossians 1:7-8), and perhaps also through Onesimus himself. The word order is unusual: “thy love and faith, which thou hast toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all saints.” Read in a crossing pattern, faith is directed toward the Lord Jesus and love toward the saints, much as Colossians 1:4 puts it. Faith may also carry the sense of faithfulness, which Philemon showed both to Christ and to his people. Either way, the point is the same: Philemon’s trust in Christ shows itself in concrete care for believers.

Love comes first in the sentence because love is what Paul is about to appeal to. He will build on it in Philemon 1:7 and name it again as the basis of his request in Philemon 1:9.

The small word “all” deserves attention. Philemon’s love reached all saints, and Paul is about to introduce a saint whom Philemon may be reluctant to include. “Saints” means those set apart as God’s own; the title rests on God’s calling, not on social rank or past record. A slave converted in a prison cell has the same title as the master in whose house the church meets. If Philemon’s love is truly toward all the saints, it must now reach Onesimus.

wordNotes.term: τὴν ἀγάπην καὶ τὴν πίστιν (tēn agapēn kai tēn pistin) — love and faith
wordNotes.explanation: Agapē is the self-giving love God shows and his people reflect; pistis is trust in God that can also include faithfulness. Paul holds them together because faith toward Christ produces love toward his people.

wordNotes.term: ἁγίους (hagious) — saints
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “holy ones,” those God has set apart for himself. The term describes all believers by virtue of God’s call, so it includes the newest convert and the humblest servant alongside respected leaders.

verses.bibleText: That the communication of thy faith may become effectual by the acknowledging of every good thing which is in you in Christ Jesus.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
This verse states the content of Paul’s prayer, and its compressed wording is among the hardest in the letter. “The communication of thy faith” translates koinōnia, the fellowship or sharing that arises from faith held in common. Philemon’s faith had drawn him into a living partnership with other believers, expressed in hospitality and generosity. Paul prays that this fellowship “may become effectual,” that is, active and productive, working itself out in fresh deeds.

The means of that effectiveness is “the acknowledging of every good thing which is in you in Christ Jesus.” Epignōsis is knowledge that grasps and acknowledges—understanding that takes hold of a truth and lives by it. The “good thing” is everything God has given his people in Christ: forgiveness, adoption, a share in one family, and the new relationships that grace creates. Some manuscripts read “in us” and others “in you,” but the sense is similar, since the good belongs to the whole believing community. The final phrase can be rendered “for Christ” or “toward Christ”: the good recognized and practiced brings honor to him and draws believers closer to him.

Paul’s prayer is not abstract. The word koinōnia anticipates the request of Philemon 1:17, where Paul asks, “If thou count me therefore a partner” (koinōnos). Philemon’s shared faith is about to meet a specific test. If he understands the good that is now present in Onesimus in Christ, his fellowship will become effective precisely in welcoming him.

So faith is meant to be shared in more than confession. It is shared at the table, in the household, and in relationships that have to be rebuilt. Knowledge of God’s gifts that never reaches such places has not yet been fully acknowledged.

wordNotes.term: ἡ κοινωνία τῆς πίστεώς σου (hē koinōnia tēs pisteōs sou) — the communication of thy faith
wordNotes.explanation: Koinōnia means participation, partnership, or sharing. Here it describes the fellowship Philemon has with others through the faith they hold in common, a fellowship that showed itself in practical generosity. The KJV “communication” carries the older sense of sharing or imparting.

wordNotes.term: ἐπιγνώσει (epignōsei) — by the acknowledging
wordNotes.explanation: Epignōsis is full or recognizing knowledge, understanding that acknowledges and responds to what it knows. Paul uses it for spiritual insight that shapes conduct, not for mere information.

verses.bibleText: For we have great joy and consolation in thy love, because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now tells Philemon what the report of his love has meant to him. The better text reads “I had,” looking back to the moment the news arrived: a prisoner received “great joy and consolation” from hearing how one of his converts was serving others. Ministry has few rewards greater than learning that those you led to Christ are living out his love.

The reason for that joy is that “the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee.” The KJV keeps the literal word; splanchna were the inward organs, which ancient speech treated as the seat of feeling, much as we speak of the heart. To refresh is to give rest and relief, the same verb Jesus uses when he promises rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28). Philemon’s hospitality, help, and encouragement had given relief to tired and burdened believers.

The verse ends with an affectionate “brother,” set at the close for emphasis. Its vocabulary is chosen with care, because each key word will return. Onesimus will be called Paul’s own splanchna (Philemon 1:12), and Paul will ask Philemon, “refresh my bowels in the Lord” (Philemon 1:20). The logic is gentle but clear: Philemon has refreshed the hearts of many saints; Onesimus is now Paul’s very heart; to refresh Paul, Philemon must receive Onesimus.

wordNotes.term: τὰ σπλάγχνα (ta splanchna) — the bowels
wordNotes.explanation: Literally the inward parts, regarded in biblical idiom as the center of compassion and affection. It is close to our use of “heart” and describes the innermost self where love is felt.

wordNotes.term: ἀναπέπαυται (anapepautai) — are refreshed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to give rest or relief, to cause someone to cease from toil or strain. The perfect tense points to refreshment that has had lasting effect among the believers Philemon served.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore, though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore” ties the appeal to the thanksgiving. Because Philemon’s love is known and proven, Paul will address him on that level. Before he does, he states plainly what he could have done instead: “though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient.” The word for boldness, parrēsia, describes the freedom and confidence to speak openly, and the verb enjoin means to give an order. Paul possessed real authority as an apostle and as the one through whom Philemon had believed. He does not pretend otherwise.

That authority is “in Christ.” Paul’s right to direct believers did not come from personality or seniority but from the commission of the Lord he served. Even so, the highest use of authority is often to hold it in reserve. Paul elsewhere refuses to lord it over the faith of believers (2 Corinthians 1:24), and Peter warns elders against domineering over the flock (1 Peter 5:3). Spiritual leadership that relies on command alone can secure compliance; it cannot produce the willing love Paul is seeking.

“That which is convenient” translates a word meaning what is fitting or proper—what belongs to a situation and is owed in it. Paul does not treat the reception of Onesimus as an optional kindness. It is the right thing for a believer to do. The only question is how Philemon will come to do it: under orders, or from a heart already moved by Christ’s love. By naming the authority he will not use, Paul honors Philemon as a mature believer and makes clear that what follows is a request of love, not a softening of duty.

wordNotes.term: τὸ ἀνῆκον (to anēkon) — that which is convenient
wordNotes.explanation: The participle describes what is fitting, proper, or required by the circumstances. The KJV “convenient” uses the older sense of suitable. Paul applies the same idea to conduct that befits those who belong to the Lord.

wordNotes.term: παρρησίαν (parrēsian) — bold
wordNotes.explanation: Parrēsia is freedom and openness of speech, the confidence to say what needs to be said without fear. Here it refers to the frankness Paul has in Christ to give a direct instruction.

verses.bibleText: Yet for love's sake I rather beseech thee, being such an one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Instead of commanding, Paul says, “for love’s sake I rather beseech thee.” The verb parakaleō means to appeal, urge, or plead. The love in view is probably both the love that binds believers together and the love Philemon has already shown (Philemon 1:5, 7). Paul places the decision on the ground where Philemon has proved himself, and in doing so he raises the stakes rather than lowering them. An order can be obeyed reluctantly. An appeal to love can be answered only by love, and refusing it would contradict the very character Paul has just praised.

Paul then describes himself: “such an one as Paul the aged.” The word presbytēs means an old man. It differs by one letter from the Greek word for ambassador, and that similarity has led to proposals that Paul meant “ambassador,” as in Ephesians 6:20. The manuscripts and the setting both support the familiar reading. Paul, likely in his late fifties or early sixties and worn by years of beatings, travel, shipwreck, and imprisonment (2 Corinthians 11:23-28), appeals as an aging man.

“And now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ” adds a second weakness to the first. The one who could command chooses to appear before Philemon as old and chained, with no leverage but love. That posture is not a mere technique of persuasion. It reflects the way of Christ, who held all authority yet took the form of a servant and won his people through self-giving (Philippians 2:5-8).

Paul’s example remains instructive for anyone with influence over others. Authority used to compel can settle a matter quickly. Authority laid aside in favor of an appeal to love calls the other person to grow, and it leaves room for a response that honors God because it is freely given.

wordNotes.term: πρεσβύτης (presbytēs) — the aged
wordNotes.explanation: The ordinary word for an old man, used of Zacharias and of the older men in Titus. It describes Paul’s stage of life and adds personal weight and vulnerability to his appeal.

wordNotes.term: διὰ τὴν ἀγάπην μᾶλλον παρακαλῶ (dia tēn agapēn mallon parakalō) — for love’s sake I rather beseech
wordNotes.explanation: Parakaleō means to urge or appeal, and mallon marks a deliberate preference. Paul chooses entreaty over command, grounding his request in love, which seeks a willing response rather than forced obedience.

verses.bibleText: I beseech thee for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now Paul names the subject of his appeal, and he does so with great care. The Greek order runs, “I appeal to you for my child, whom I have begotten in my bonds, Onesimus.” The name comes last. Before Philemon hears the name that might stir resentment, he hears that the person in question is Paul’s own child, born to him spiritually in prison. Philemon meets Onesimus first through Paul’s affection and only then through his own memories.

“My son” translates teknon, a tender word for a child. Paul often used parental language for those he brought to Christ. He told the Corinthians that though they had many instructors, he had begotten them through the gospel (1 Corinthians 4:15), and he spoke of laboring in birth for the Galatians until Christ was formed in them (Galatians 4:19). Timothy and Titus are also called his children in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2; Titus 1:4).

“Whom I have begotten in my bonds” locates this new birth in the place of Paul’s confinement. The prison, which might have ended his usefulness, became a birthplace. Scripture does not tell us how a runaway slave from Colossae came to Paul’s side—whether by chance, by need, or by deliberately seeking out his master’s friend—but the outcome was conversion. God’s providence brought together an apostle in chains and a fugitive who had nowhere else to turn.

Onesimus’s identity has therefore changed. Before he is a legal problem or a household loss, he is a member of God’s family. He is also, like Philemon, one of Paul’s children (compare Philemon 1:19), which makes the two men brothers through the same spiritual father. The gospel creates a kinship that runs straight across the social line between owner and owned. Those who have wronged us, once they belong to Christ, must first be seen as his.

wordNotes.term: τοῦ ἐμοῦ τέκνου (tou emou teknou) — my son
wordNotes.explanation: Teknon is a child, and the emphatic possessive “my own” stresses closeness. Paul uses the word for converts he regards with a parent’s love and responsibility, placing Onesimus alongside Timothy and Titus as his spiritual offspring.

wordNotes.term: ἐγέννησα (egennēsa) — I have begotten
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to father or give birth. Applied to conversion, it describes the new life that comes through the gospel. Paul is the instrument; the life itself is God’s gift through his word and Spirit.

verses.bibleText: Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Onesimus was a common slave name meaning “useful” or “beneficial,” and Paul plays on it: “in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me.” The words achrēstos and euchrēstos mean useless and useful. Onesimus had not lived up to his name. Whether through poor service, through running away, or through taking what was not his, he had been worth little to Philemon. Paul does not excuse that past; he sets it beside the present.

In the pronunciation of the period, chrēstos sounded nearly the same as Christos. The wordplay may therefore carry a further hint: the man who was without use has become useful through Christ. Whether or not Paul intended that echo, the transformation is the point. “But now” marks the turning point of conversion. Onesimus has become what his name always promised, because grace has made him new.

The usefulness reaches both men: “to thee and to me.” Paul has already benefited from Onesimus’s service in prison, and Philemon will benefit from a changed servant and brother. Paul thus links himself to Onesimus’s future, so that whatever Philemon does for him he does also for Paul. The same adjective appears later when Paul asks for Mark, once a deserter, because he is “profitable to me for the ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). God specializes in making the useless serviceable and the failed fruitful, so that they become vessels “meet for the master’s use” (2 Timothy 2:21).

wordNotes.term: ἄχρηστον … εὔχρηστον (achrēston … euchrēston) — unprofitable … profitable
wordNotes.explanation: The two adjectives mean useless and useful, and together they echo the meaning of Onesimus’s name. Paul contrasts what Onesimus was before conversion with what he has become in Christ.

verses.bibleText: Whom I have sent again: thou therefore receive him, that is, mine own bowels:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Whom I have sent again” uses the verb anapempō, to send back. The tense is the kind letter writers used to describe what would be past by the time the letter was read, so it means “I am sending him back” with this letter. Onesimus traveled with Tychicus, who carried the Colossian letter and was charged to tell the church of Paul’s affairs (Colossians 4:7-9). The words “thou therefore receive him” are missing from the earliest manuscripts; the formal request comes in Philemon 1:17.

Paul describes Onesimus as “mine own bowels,” the same word he used for the hearts Philemon refreshed (Philemon 1:7). In sending Onesimus, Paul is sending part of himself. The return cost both men something. Onesimus was walking back into the power of a master who, by law, could punish him severely. Paul was giving up a companion who had become dear and helpful to him. Repentance led Onesimus to face the one he had wronged, yet he did not go alone or unprotected; he went with Paul’s love written beside his name.

By identifying Onesimus with his own heart, Paul ensures that how Philemon treats the slave will be how he treats the apostle. That pattern reflects the way Christ identifies with his people. What is done to the least of his brethren is done to him (Matthew 25:40), and those who persecute his followers persecute him (Acts 9:4-5).

wordNotes.term: ἀνέπεμψα (anepempsa) — I have sent again
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to send back or to send up to a higher authority. Here it refers to returning Onesimus to Philemon, written from the standpoint of the reader for whom the sending will already have happened.

wordNotes.term: τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα (ta ema splanchna) — mine own bowels
wordNotes.explanation: Paul calls Onesimus his very heart, his inward self. The expression shows intense affection and identification, so that receiving Onesimus becomes receiving the one who loves him.

verses.bibleText: Whom I would have retained with me, that in thy stead he might have ministered unto me in the bonds of the gospel:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul admits what he would have preferred: “Whom I would have retained with me.” The imperfect tense suggests a wish he had carried for some time, weighing whether to keep Onesimus. The reason was practical and spiritual: “that in thy stead he might have ministered unto me in the bonds of the gospel.” A prisoner depended on friends for food, errands, writing materials, and companionship, and Onesimus had proved himself useful in exactly these ways. He may also have served as a messenger in Paul’s gospel work.

“In thy stead” is a graceful touch. Paul assumes that Philemon himself would gladly have served him had he been present, so Onesimus’s help could be counted as Philemon’s own service rendered through his representative. The phrase honors Philemon and invites him to see Onesimus as a partner in his own care for Paul. “The bonds of the gospel” reminds him again of Paul’s chains and of the cause that produced them; loyalty to the gospel often costs those who carry it.

Yet Paul did not keep Onesimus. However good his purpose, he would not hold back what rightly belonged to another without that person’s consent. The gospel’s advance did not give him license to bypass Philemon. Good ends do not excuse disregard for the rights and conscience of others, and Paul’s restraint here shows integrity in the use of influence.

wordNotes.term: ὑπὲρ σοῦ (hyper sou) — in thy stead
wordNotes.explanation: Hyper with the genitive can mean on behalf of or in place of. Paul pictures Onesimus serving as Philemon’s representative, supplying help that Philemon would have offered in person.

wordNotes.term: διακονῇ (diakonē) — he might have ministered
wordNotes.explanation: The verb diakoneō means to serve or wait upon someone. It covers practical care as well as service in the work of the gospel, and it is the word Jesus uses for his own life of service.

verses.bibleText: But without thy mind would I do nothing; that thy benefit should not be as it were of necessity, but willingly.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But without thy mind would I do nothing.” The word translated mind, gnōmē, means judgment or consent. Paul was confident Philemon would approve, yet he refused to presume. He would not make a decision that belonged to Philemon, even one he was sure was good. Respect for another person’s right to choose governed his conduct.

The purpose follows: “that thy benefit should not be as it were of necessity, but willingly.” The “benefit” is the good deed Philemon would do, whether in releasing Onesimus to serve Paul or in some other act of kindness. Paul wanted that good to arise freely. Had he kept Onesimus and informed Philemon afterward, Philemon would have been left with no real choice; his generosity would have been extracted rather than offered. The phrase “as it were” shows how careful Paul is: he wants to avoid even the appearance of compulsion.

The principle runs throughout Scripture. The tabernacle was built from offerings given by everyone whose heart made him willing (Exodus 25:2). God loves a cheerful giver, not one who gives grudgingly or of necessity (2 Corinthians 9:7). Elders are to shepherd willingly, not by constraint (1 Peter 5:2). God himself does not force love, for love that is forced is no longer love. His government rests on freely given loyalty, and he seeks worshipers who choose him. Paul’s method in this letter mirrors that divine pattern.

There is still pressure in the letter—Paul is open about his wishes—but it is the pressure of a relationship and of truth, not of coercion. Philemon is left free to respond, and that freedom is what makes his response meaningful.

wordNotes.term: κατὰ ἑκούσιον (kata hekousion) — willingly
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase means of one’s own free will, voluntarily. It stands opposite kata anankēn, “by necessity” or under compulsion. Scripture repeatedly values offerings and service that spring from a willing heart.

wordNotes.term: χωρὶς τῆς σῆς γνώμης (chōris tēs sēs gnōmēs) — without thy mind
wordNotes.explanation: Gnōmē is judgment, opinion, or consent. Paul refuses to act apart from Philemon’s considered decision, treating him as a responsible partner rather than a subordinate to be managed.

verses.bibleText: For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now steps back to view the whole episode from God’s side. “For perhaps” is a word of humility. Paul does not claim to know for certain why events unfolded as they did, and he does not baptize Onesimus’s flight as a holy act. Yet he invites Philemon to consider that a larger purpose may have been at work.

The verb is significant. Paul does not say “he ran away” but “he therefore departed,” literally “he was separated.” The passive voice softens the description without denying the wrong, and it leaves room for the hand of God behind the human choice. Scripture often speaks this way. Joseph told his brothers that although they had meant evil against him, God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20), and he could say it was God who sent him ahead to preserve life (Genesis 45:5-8). The brothers remained guilty, yet God overruled their sin for blessing. In the same manner Onesimus’s departure, whatever its motives, carried him to the place where he heard the gospel.

The contrast of times is striking: “for a season” and “for ever.” Literally Paul says “for an hour,” a short span measured against the lasting relationship that has resulted. The verb translated “receive” means to have back in full, as one receives payment that settles an account. Philemon lost a slave for a while; he is receiving back a brother permanently. The word aiōnios here describes a relationship that will not end with this life, because both men now share the life Christ gives, which will be theirs fully at the resurrection.

The Law spoke of a servant who chose to stay with his master “for ever” (Exodus 21:6). Paul’s “for ever” is of a different kind. It is not bondage made permanent but brotherhood made permanent. This is the way God often works: a loss we regret becomes the occasion for a gain we could not have planned, though it never makes the wrong itself right. Discerning that pattern calls for Paul’s own humility—“perhaps”—and for trust that God “worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Ephesians 1:11) and makes them serve the good of those who love him.

wordNotes.term: ἐχωρίσθη (echōristhē) — he departed
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “he was separated.” The passive form describes Onesimus’s leaving without blaming or excusing him outright and opens the possibility that God was at work in the separation, as in Joseph’s story.

wordNotes.term: αἰώνιον αὐτὸν ἀπέχῃς (aiōnion auton apechēs) — that thou shouldest receive him for ever
wordNotes.explanation: Apechō means to receive in full, a term used in receipts for payment. Aiōnion means lasting or age-long; here it describes a bond in Christ that continues beyond this life rather than a permanent enslavement.

verses.bibleText: Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
This verse is the heart of the letter. Philemon is to receive Onesimus “not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved.” The Greek says “no longer as a slave,” which signals that the old way of regarding Onesimus is to end. “Above a servant” means more than a slave, beyond what that category can contain. Paul uses for Onesimus the same words he has used for Philemon—“brother” (Philemon 1:7, 20) and “beloved” (Philemon 1:1).

The next phrase prevents this change from being merely inward: “specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord.” He is dear to Paul, and dearer still to Philemon, who will live beside him daily. “In the Lord” describes their spiritual relationship as fellow believers. “In the flesh” describes their ordinary, earthly relationship—household, work, and daily life. Paul expects the brotherhood to reach both. A master cannot call a man a beloved brother at the Lord’s table and then treat him as property in the kitchen. The new relationship must reshape the old one from within.

Paul stops short of an explicit command to free Onesimus, consistent with his refusal to order Philemon about. But the logic of the verse presses in that direction, and the hope that Philemon would do “more than I say” (Philemon 1:21) points the same way. The New Testament called for no armed revolt, which in that world would have meant slaughter for slaves. It did something more far-reaching: it declared that in Christ there is “neither bond nor free” (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11), urged slaves to gain their freedom when possible (1 Corinthians 7:21), condemned “menstealers” among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), and placed masters and slaves together under one Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9).

These convictions grow from deep roots. Every person bears God’s image (Genesis 1:27). Israel’s story began with God freeing slaves from Egypt, and his law made kidnapping a man to sell him a capital crime (Exodus 21:16). The trajectory of Scripture runs steadily against slavery. A church in which master and slave share one table, call one another brother, and may serve under a slave as elder has already undermined the claim that one human can own another. Using this letter to defend slavery, as some later did, turns its message upside down.

At the center of it all stands Christ. Every believer was once a slave to sin and has been made a son and heir through him (Galatians 4:7). The grace that adopted Philemon now requires him to embrace his brother.

wordNotes.term: οὐκέτι ὡς δοῦλον ἀλλ’ ὑπὲρ δοῦλον (ouketi hōs doulon all’ hyper doulon) — not now as a servant, but above a servant
wordNotes.explanation: Ouketi means “no longer,” marking the end of a former state, and hyper with the accusative means “beyond” or “more than.” Doulos is a slave, not merely a hired servant. Paul says Onesimus can no longer be regarded primarily through the category of slave, because his identity now surpasses it.

wordNotes.term: ἀδελφὸν ἀγαπητόν (adelphon agapēton) — a brother beloved
wordNotes.explanation: The same pair of words Paul uses of Tychicus and of Onesimus in Colossians. A brother belongs to the same family, and beloved marks the affection that family should show. The title gives Onesimus equal standing with his master before God.

verses.bibleText: If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here, after a long and careful approach, comes the first direct request of the letter: “receive him as myself.” The condition that introduces it—“if thou count me therefore a partner”—is the kind of conditional sentence that assumes the case is true. Paul is not doubting their bond; he is appealing to it. Since Philemon regards him as a partner, he should act accordingly.

The word partner, koinōnos, is related to the koinōnia of Philemon 1:6. Paul prayed that the fellowship of Philemon’s faith would become effective; now he shows where that effectiveness is to appear. Partnership with Paul is not a private friendship between two men. It is a shared life in Christ that includes everyone Paul calls his own. Philemon cannot claim fellowship with the apostle while shutting out the one Paul calls his very heart.

“Receive” translates proslambanō, to welcome someone into one’s company and fellowship. It is the word Paul uses when he tells believers to receive one another as Christ also received them (Romans 15:7). The measure of the welcome is Paul himself. If Paul arrived at Colossae, Philemon would honor him, house him, seat him at his table, and treat him as a dear brother and spiritual father. That is how Onesimus is to be treated—with no probation, no lesser place, no lingering suspicion.

The request echoes the gospel. Jesus told his disciples that whoever received them received him (Matthew 10:40). At a still higher level, God receives sinners for Christ’s sake, so that believers are “accepted in the beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). The Father does not welcome the repentant on the basis of their record but on the basis of his Son’s standing. Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus on the basis of Paul’s standing. Every believer who has been received in this way is called to extend the same welcome to others.

wordNotes.term: κοινωνόν (koinōnon) — a partner
wordNotes.explanation: A koinōnos is a sharer or associate, one who participates with another in a common life or enterprise. It can describe business partners and, among believers, those who share in Christ and in his work.

wordNotes.term: προσλαβοῦ (proslabou) — receive
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative of proslambanō, to take to oneself, to welcome into one’s home or fellowship. Paul uses it for the warm acceptance believers owe one another because Christ has accepted them.

verses.bibleText: If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul anticipates the obstacle that might hinder the welcome. “If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought” is tactfully phrased. Paul does not accuse Onesimus of theft in front of the church, but the possibility is plain. At the very least, his absence had cost Philemon the value of his labor; he may also have taken money or goods to fund his escape. A Christian master could reasonably feel that justice required compensation before reconciliation.

Paul’s answer is remarkable: “put that on mine account.” The verb elloga is a bookkeeping term meaning to charge to someone’s account. Paul assumes the debt himself. He neither denies that a debt exists nor asks Philemon to pretend nothing happened. Scripture takes restitution seriously. The Law required one who had wronged a neighbor in property to restore it with an added fifth (Leviticus 6:2-5), and Zacchaeus’s conversion showed itself in his promise to repay those he had defrauded (Luke 19:8). Reconciliation in the gospel does not cancel justice by ignoring it. It satisfies justice by having someone bear the cost.

That is why this verse has long been read as a living parable of the atonement. The debt of sin is real, and the sinner cannot pay it. Christ, who owed nothing, takes the debt on himself. God made him “to be sin for us, who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21); the handwriting that stood against us he took away, “nailing it to his cross” (Colossians 2:14). The same accounting language appears when Paul says that sin is not “imputed” where there is no law (Romans 5:13) and when he describes the blessedness of the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin (Romans 4:8). As Paul stood between Onesimus and his master, Christ stands between the sinner and the Father.

Paul is not a savior, and his pledge does not atone. But his act shows what grace looks like when it moves into a human relationship. Philemon was to look at Onesimus and see Paul’s promise rather than the old wrong. The forgiven are taught to look at one another in the same way, seeing Christ’s payment where they once saw only debt.

wordNotes.term: ἐλλόγα (elloga) — put that on mine account
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative of ellogaō, a commercial term meaning to enter into the account or charge to someone. Paul asks that Onesimus’s debt be recorded against his own name.

wordNotes.term: ἠδίκησεν (ēdikēsen) — hath wronged
wordNotes.explanation: Adikeō means to do wrong or injustice, often with the sense of causing loss or harm. The word acknowledges that Onesimus may have injured Philemon, which Paul does not minimize.

verses.bibleText: I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now writes a formal pledge: “I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it.” Whether he wrote the whole letter himself or took the pen from a secretary at this point, the effect is the same. A signed statement in one’s own handwriting was a binding acknowledgment of debt in the ancient world. The verb for repay, apotinō, is a legal term for paying compensation. Paul is not speaking loosely; he is giving Philemon an enforceable promise.

Then comes a sudden turn: “albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides.” By saying that he will not mention something, Paul mentions it. The figure is gentle and probably carries a touch of affectionate humor. Philemon had come to faith through Paul’s ministry, so he owed Paul his very self, his new life in Christ. Paul is not cancelling his pledge or slipping out of it; his promise to pay stands. But he sets Onesimus’s debt beside a much larger account.

The effect is to rearrange the ledger. Whatever Onesimus owes Philemon is small next to what Philemon owes Paul, and what Philemon owes Paul is small next to what both owe God. Jesus told of a servant forgiven an immense debt who then seized a fellow servant over a trifling sum; the master’s question was, “Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?” (Matthew 18:33). Those who know how much they have been forgiven are able to forgive (Luke 7:47). Gratitude for grace received becomes the ground of grace extended. The only debt that should remain among believers is the continuing debt of love (Romans 13:8).

wordNotes.term: ἔγραψα τῇ ἐμῇ χειρί (egrapsa tē emē cheiri) — I have written it with mine own hand
wordNotes.explanation: Paul’s handwritten line served as a personal signature and guarantee. Elsewhere he adds his own hand to authenticate a letter; here it turns his offer into a signed promissory note.

wordNotes.term: σεαυτόν μοι προσοφείλεις (seauton moi prosopheileis) — thou owest unto me even thine own self besides
wordNotes.explanation: Prosopheilō means to owe in addition. Philemon owes Paul a further and greater debt: his own self, because his life in Christ came through Paul’s gospel ministry.

verses.bibleText: Yea, brother, let me have joy of thee in the Lord: refresh my bowels in the Lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Yea, brother” presses gently toward a favorable answer, and the address “brother” returns once more. Paul continues, “let me have joy of thee in the Lord.” The verb onaimēn means to have benefit or profit from someone, and it sounds very close to the name Onesimus. Paul seems to be saying, in effect, “Let me find you useful, Philemon—be an Onesimus to me.” The benefit he seeks is “in the Lord”: not money or comfort, but the spiritual joy of seeing Christ’s love at work among his converts.

The second line echoes Philemon 1:7: “refresh my bowels in the Lord.” Philemon had refreshed the hearts of many saints, and Paul asks for that same refreshment for himself. Since he has already called Onesimus his own heart (Philemon 1:12), the way to refresh Paul is plain. Welcoming Onesimus is the gift that will lift the old prisoner’s spirit. A minister’s deepest joy is not his own ease but the sight of those he has led to Christ walking together in love (3 John 1:4; Philippians 2:2).

wordNotes.term: ὀναίμην (onaimēn) — let me have joy
wordNotes.explanation: A rare optative form of oninēmi, to derive benefit or help. It shares its sound and sense with the name Onesimus, forming a gentle wordplay: Paul hopes to profit from Philemon as Philemon will profit from Onesimus.

wordNotes.term: ἀνάπαυσόν μου τὰ σπλάγχνα (anapauson mou ta splanchna) — refresh my bowels
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative of the same verb used in Philemon 1:7, joined to the word for the inner self. Paul asks Philemon to give his heart rest and relief by acting on his request.

verses.bibleText: Having confidence in thy obedience I wrote unto thee, knowing that thou wilt also do more than I say.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul closes his appeal with an expression of trust: “Having confidence in thy obedience I wrote unto thee.” The word obedience may seem surprising after Paul has insisted that he will not command (Philemon 1:8-9). But the obedience in view is not submission to Paul’s personal orders. It is Philemon’s response to the will of God made known through the gospel and through the apostle’s appeal. Paul elsewhere speaks of “obedience to the faith” (Romans 1:5; 16:26), the trusting surrender that grace produces. Faith that receives Christ goes on to do what Christ’s love requires.

“Knowing that thou wilt also do more than I say” lifts the request beyond its stated limits. The phrase hyper ha legō, “beyond what I say,” uses the same preposition as “above a servant” in Philemon 1:16. Paul has asked only that Onesimus be received as Paul himself would be. What could “more” mean? It could mean forgiving any debt despite Paul’s pledge, or returning Onesimus to Paul to serve in the gospel, as the wish of Philemon 1:13 suggests. Most naturally, given “both in the flesh, and in the Lord,” it includes granting Onesimus his freedom. Paul leaves the specifics to Philemon, but the direction is unmistakable.

This restraint fits Paul’s method. The gospel did not abolish slavery by decree in the first century, yet it set in motion principles that would prove fatal to it. A master who receives his slave as a beloved brother and goes beyond what is asked has already begun to dismantle the relationship of ownership. Change that begins in converted hearts and redeemed communities reaches further and lasts longer than change imposed from outside.

Love never aims at the minimum. Jesus taught his followers to go the second mile (Matthew 5:41) and reminded them that doing only what is commanded leaves us “unprofitable servants” (Luke 17:10). Grace does not ask, “How little may I do?” but “What more can love do here?” Paul’s confidence in Philemon is also a call to every believer whose obedience springs from gratitude: let the response to Christ exceed the letter of the request.

wordNotes.term: τῇ ὑπακοῇ σου (tē hypakoē sou) — thy obedience
wordNotes.explanation: Hypakoē is responsive hearing that becomes action. In Paul it often describes the response of faith to God’s word rather than mere compliance with a human superior, so Philemon’s obedience is ultimately directed to the Lord.

wordNotes.term: ὑπὲρ ἃ λέγω (hyper ha legō) — more than I say
wordNotes.explanation: Hyper with the accusative means “beyond” or “over and above.” Paul expects Philemon to exceed the explicit request, leaving room for generosity that goes beyond a merely correct response.

verses.bibleText: But withal prepare me also a lodging: for I trust that through your prayers I shall be given unto you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But withal prepare me also a lodging.” The word xenia means a guest room or hospitality. Paul expected to be released and hoped to visit Colossae, as he likewise expected to see the Philippians again (Philippians 1:25-26; 2:24). The request expresses confidence in his friend’s welcome. It also carries a gentle note of accountability: Paul will come and see for himself how Onesimus has been received.

The ground of his hope is prayer: “I trust that through your prayers I shall be given unto you.” The pronouns are plural again, so the whole house church is praying for him. The verb, charisthēsomai, comes from the word for grace. Paul’s release, if it comes, will be God’s gracious gift in answer to his people’s intercession, much as Peter’s release came while the church prayed (Acts 12:5). The apostle did not see prayer as a pious extra but as a means God uses to accomplish his purposes. The later letters to Timothy and Titus suggest that this hope was fulfilled and that Paul was freed for a further season of travel before his final imprisonment.

wordNotes.term: χαρισθήσομαι (charisthēsomai) — I shall be given
wordNotes.explanation: From charizomai, to give freely or graciously, related to charis, grace. Paul regards his possible release and return to his friends as a favor God would grant in response to prayer.

wordNotes.term: ξενίαν (xenian) — a lodging
wordNotes.explanation: Xenia refers to hospitality or a guest room prepared for a visitor. The request assumes the warm welcome that Christian homes extended to traveling ministers.

verses.bibleText: There salute thee Epaphras, my fellowprisoner in Christ Jesus;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Greetings begin with Epaphras, the one name in the list Philemon knew best. Epaphras was a Colossian who first brought the gospel to that city and probably to nearby Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 1:7; 4:12-13). He had come to Paul with news of the churches and now labored for them in prayer from a distance, “always labouring fervently” that they might stand complete in the will of God.

Paul calls him “my fellowprisoner in Christ Jesus.” The word means a fellow captive, originally a prisoner of war. Epaphras may have been arrested with Paul, or he may have voluntarily shared Paul’s confinement in order to serve him. Either way, he stood with the apostle in his chains. His greeting reminds Philemon that the man who founded his church was bound to the same cause and shared the same cost. The appeal on behalf of Onesimus thus comes not from Paul alone but from a circle of faithful workers, including Philemon’s own pastor.

wordNotes.term: συναιχμάλωτός (synaichmalōtos) — fellowprisoner
wordNotes.explanation: Literally a fellow captive taken by the spear, a prisoner of war. Paul uses it for coworkers who shared his imprisonment, picturing the gospel ministry as a campaign in which its servants may be taken captive.

verses.bibleText: Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Four more coworkers send greetings: “Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers.” Each name carries a story. Marcus is John Mark, who years earlier had turned back from the first missionary journey, so that Paul refused to take him on the second (Acts 13:13; 15:37-39). Now he stands at Paul’s side as a fellow worker, and later Paul will ask for him because he is “profitable to me for the ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11), using the very word applied to Onesimus in Philemon 1:11. In a letter about a man once useless and now useful, Mark’s presence is itself a testimony to restoration. Paul, who once refused Mark, had learned to receive him again, and so he could ask Philemon to do the same for Onesimus.

Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, had been seized in the riot at Ephesus and later sailed with Paul toward Rome (Acts 19:29; 27:2); Colossians calls him a fellow prisoner (Colossians 4:10). Luke, “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), traveled with Paul for years and would remain with him to the end (2 Timothy 4:11).

Demas sounds a sober note. He is listed here among faithful workers, yet Paul later writes that Demas forsook him, “having loved this present world” (2 Timothy 4:10). Nearness to faithful ministry did not guarantee perseverance. Together these names show the range of the Christian company: one restored after failure, one steadfast through danger, one faithful to the last, and one who would later turn away. Every believer is called to finish the course in dependence on the grace that began it.

wordNotes.term: οἱ συνεργοί μου (hoi synergoi mou) — my fellowlabourers
wordNotes.explanation: The plural of the word used for Philemon in Philemon 1:1. By grouping these men with Philemon as coworkers, Paul places the recipient within a wide fellowship of service.

wordNotes.term: Μᾶρκος (Markos) — Marcus
wordNotes.explanation: John Mark, cousin of Barnabas, whose early departure caused a sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas. His later service with Paul shows that a failure need not be final.

verses.bibleText: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter ends where it began, with grace: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” The pronoun is plural, so the blessing rests on Philemon, his household, and the whole church that has heard the letter read. “Your spirit” is a familiar Pauline way of speaking of the person in his inner life before God; it is a prayer that grace will be present in the whole of their life together.

The framing is fitting. Grace opened the letter (Philemon 1:3) and grace closes it, enclosing the entire appeal. Only grace could move a wronged master to welcome a runaway as his brother, and only grace could give a slave the courage to go home. What Paul has asked of Philemon is beyond ordinary human kindness, so he commits him to the favor of the Lord Jesus, which supplies what it requires. The same grace that carried the letter to Colossae is offered to every reader who must still forgive, return, or welcome someone home. A word of grace ends the letter because grace alone can finish what the letter asks.

wordNotes.term: μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν (meta tou pneumatos hymōn) — with your spirit
wordNotes.explanation: A benediction formula in which “spirit” refers to the inner person in relationship with God. It is equivalent to “with you,” with emphasis on the life that grace sustains from within.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What happens to an old relationship of power when both people come to belong to the same Lord?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The gospel that made Onesimus Paul’s child and Philemon’s brother requires a welcome that reshapes even the master–slave relationship, and Paul models that welcome by bearing the cost himself.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul choose to appeal rather than command, and what does that choice ask of Philemon?
How does the phrase “both in the flesh, and in the Lord” keep the change in Onesimus’s standing from being merely spiritual?
In what ways does Paul’s offer to pay Onesimus’s debt picture what Christ has done for sinners?
What does the letter teach about the place of restitution in reconciliation?
Why does it matter that the letter was read before the whole house church?
commonMisunderstandings: The letter does not endorse slavery; it plants a kinship in Christ that cannot coexist with treating a brother as property.
Paul’s gentle tone does not make the request optional; appealing to love raises the claim rather than lowering it.
Seeing God’s hand in Onesimus’s separation does not excuse the wrong; Paul still provides for the debt to be paid.
Forgiveness here is not pretending nothing happened; someone bears the cost so that the wrongdoer can be received.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the personal and the social together: a returning slave is welcomed as a brother, and that welcome reaches into the household, the church, and finally the very structure that held him.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Receive those whom Christ has received, even those who once wronged you, and be willing to bear a cost so that reconciliation can happen.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: As Paul took Onesimus’s debt on himself so that he could be welcomed home, Christ bears the sinner’s debt so that the repentant are received by the Father as members of his family.
flow: Like Onesimus, every sinner has run from the Master and incurred a debt he cannot pay.
Christ meets us in our flight and gives us new birth into God’s family.
He places our debt on his own account and pays it at the cross.
We are received by the Father as Christ himself is received.
Those received in this way go back to make right what they can and to welcome others as brothers.
simpleIllustrations: A runaway carries home a letter in his benefactor’s own handwriting: “Whatever he owes, charge it to me.”
A guest arrives with a recommendation from your dearest friend, who writes, “Treat him as you would treat me.”
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you let Christ put your debt on his account and return to the Father as one received for his sake?
cautions: Do not use the letter to suggest that the gospel is indifferent to oppression or injustice.
Do not present Paul’s substitution as identical to Christ’s atonement; it is a living picture, not a saving act.
Do not imply that being forgiven removes the duty to make restitution where it is possible.

reflectionQuestions: Whom have I been slow to receive as a brother or sister because of an old wrong or a social difference?
Where do I prefer to command or pressure when love would appeal and wait for a willing response?
What debt has Christ placed on his own account for me, and how should that shape the way I handle what others owe me?
Is there a wrong I need to return and make right, trusting that grace goes with me?
How might God be working a lasting good through a separation or failure I still regret?
